title: Trump Targets Alaska: New Frontier in His Election Power Grab, Politico Reports
body:
Washington – The Justice Department has filed a sweeping legal challenge that could invalidate Alaska’s Senate election results if Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan is defeated, a move that has stunned officials from both parties and underscored President Donald Trump’s expanding effort to shape the nation’s electoral outcomes ahead of the 2024 midterms.

The lawsuit, lodged by the Department of Justice (DOJ) under the Trump administration, alleges irregularities in Alaska’s voting procedures and seeks a federal injunction that would halt the certification of the Senate race. If successful, the filing would effectively prevent Alaska’s voters from determining their representation in the upper chamber, a step that political analysts say represents an unprecedented level of federal intervention in a state’s electoral process.

The filing arrives at a moment when the Republican Party is gearing up for what many anticipate will be a contentious midterm election cycle. Senate races across the country have already become focal points for national parties, with both Democrats and Republicans pouring resources into competitive contests. Alaska, long considered a reliably Republican stronghold, has emerged as a potential flashpoint after polling indicated a narrowing gap between Sullivan and his Democratic challenger, former Anchorage mayor Dan Berman. The DOJ’s preemptive action—issued before any votes have been tallied—signals a willingness to use federal authority to protect incumbents perceived as aligned with the administration’s agenda.

Legal experts warn that the lawsuit raises serious constitutional questions. The Department of Justice’s authority to intervene in state election certification is limited, and critics argue that the filing bypasses the traditional role of state courts and election officials. “This is a direct challenge to the principle of state sovereignty in administering elections,” said constitutional law professor Elena Ramirez of Georgetown University. “If the federal government can unilaterally block a state’s election results, it sets a dangerous precedent that could be weaponized in future contests.”

State officials in Alaska have pushed back, with Governor Mike Dunleavy, a Republican, issuing a statement that the lawsuit is “an unwarranted intrusion into Alaska’s democratic process.” Democratic leaders, including Alaska’s Secretary of State, have filed their own counter-lawsuits, asserting that the DOJ’s claims lack merit and that any attempt to nullify the election would violate both state and federal law. The bipartisan outcry reflects a broader concern that the Trump administration’s aggressive legal strategy could erode public confidence in the integrity of elections nationwide.

The controversy also highlights the broader strategy employed by President Trump and his allies to contest unfavorable outcomes. Since the 2020 presidential election, the administration has pursued a series of legal challenges, legislative proposals, and executive actions aimed at tightening control over voting mechanisms, from mail‑in ballot restrictions to changes in poll worker certification. The Alaska case represents the latest extension of that playbook, targeting a Senate race that could influence the balance of power in Congress.

Looking ahead, the fate of the DOJ’s lawsuit will likely be decided by the federal courts, with a ruling expected before Alaska’s scheduled certification deadline in early December. Should the court deny the injunction, the state will proceed with its usual certification process, and the race will be decided by the voters. If the injunction is granted, the decision could be appealed all the way to the Supreme Court, potentially delaying Alaska’s representation in the Senate for months. Regardless of the outcome, the episode is poised to become a litmus test for the limits of federal involvement in state elections and may shape the legal landscape for future contests across the country.
